chunks: RISC vs CISC advantages. The question: What are some advantages of RISC vs CISC?
RISC and CISC are two styles of instruction set. RISC uses a small set of simple instructions that are all the same size, and only loads and stores touch memory.
CISC has richer instructions of varying size, and one can do several things, like adding a number straight from memory.
RISC's advantages are mostly in hardware: simpler decoding, cleaner pipelines and smaller control logic.
Think of giving directions. RISC says: "walk one block, turn left, walk one block". Each step is simple and quick to understand.
CISC says: "go to the library", which is one short instruction, but the listener must work out many steps. Short directions save paper.
Simple steps are easier for a pipeline to handle in an assembly-line way.
The two top rows show why CISC is paid for in the front end. After decode, both styles feed a similar out-of-order engine.
The x86 path needs extra stages (and often a micro-op cache so the expensive decode can be skipped on hot loops), which costs power.
Load/store architecture: only load and store instructions access memory. Everything else works on registers. Decode: working out what an instruction asks for.
Same-size instructions make this easy. Micro-op: a simple internal step. Modern x86 chips split complex instructions into these. Code density: how compactly a program is encoded.
CPI: average cycles per instruction ("Characterizing CPU performance").
Take "add register R2 to the value in memory at A". CISC does it in 1 instruction. RISC takes 3: load, add, store.
With the page's teaching numbers, a CISC program has 10 to the 9 instructions at CPI 2. 2, and a RISC program has 1. 4 times 10 to the 9 at CPI 1. 1, both on a 2 gigahertz clock.
CISC takes 1. 10 seconds and RISC takes 0. 77 seconds. RISC has 40% more instructions but half the CPI. That is the whole idea: RISC trades more instructions for simpler hardware.
"RISC uses simple, fixed-length, load/store instructions with lots of registers.
That makes decode cheap and pipelining clean, so you get low CPI, a fast clock and less area and power.
CISC packs more work into each instruction and has better code density, which lowers instruction count. By the Iron Law it's a trade between IC and CPI.
Today x86 translates to micro-ops internally, so the difference is mostly the cost of the front end."
